newsitem.title: INDIA: India sees consumer goods import barriers removed.
newsitem.headline: India sees consumer goods import barriers removed.

text.p: Indian Finance Secretary Montek Singh Ahluwalia said on Monday that he believed all import restrictions on consumer goods would be removed within a few years.
Ahluwalia told a conference on competition policy in the Indian capital that quantitative restrictions remained on a broad range of imported consumer goods.
"It is the declared policy of the government of India that these restrictions will be phased out over a period," he said.
He said that in the past two to three years, there had been a perceptible shift in India, and a significant number of consumer goods sectors had been opened up to imports.
"Within a fairly short space of time, a few years, it would be possible to eliminate all remaining restrictive barriers to trade," he said.
Ahluwalia said India had begun opening up infrastructure sectors such as telecommunications, airports, ports, roads and power to private competition, but much more remained to be done.

"I'm quite hopeful that in the next few years many of these problems will be overcome and we will in fact see a lot more private sector competition in these traditional, so-called monopoly areas," he said.
The finance secretary said India had to balance the need to deregulate state-controlled sectors with the need to regulate competition.
He said that sometimes it could be more important to remove restrictions impeding competition than to impose new regulations.
Ahluwalia cited the area of mergers, which were commonly believed to reduce competition. However, in India mergers may result from increased competition and internal restructuring, he said.
"Our own experience of regulators is not that they are all-knowing, all-wise," Ahluwalia said.

"So I have some doubts about whether premature imposition of restrictive systems will in fact impede what might well be the natural restructuring of industry at a time when external and other barriers to competition, internal as well as external, are being lowered," he said.

"A fledgling industry that is about to be created would be subject to a whole lot of potentially, possibly viable but supposedly competition-enhancing rules which may in fact prevent the establishment of a strong industry," he said.
